body:
What was revolutionary nationalism abroad?

In the early 20th century, some Indian nationalists believed that British rule could not be ended merely by submitting petitions for reform. They demanded freedom from colonial control and favoured stronger forms of resistance. The Swadeshi movement, which expanded after the partition of Bengal in 1905, gave further force to these ideas. Some activists advocated revolutionary action, while others focused on spreading nationalist arguments through writing, speeches and political associations.

When Indian nationalists carried this work beyond India, it became an overseas dimension of the Indian national movement. It was not a single party. Different groups worked in Britain, continental Europe and North America, often sharing the aim of Indian independence without having the same leaders or methods.

Why were centres formed outside India?

Working abroad made it possible to meet Indian students, emigrant workers and foreign supporters. Activists circulated printed arguments against colonial rule and helped organise Indians living overseas. Their experiences also differed by place: Indian students in London encountered political debates at the centre of the British Empire, while Indian migrants on the Pacific Coast of North America faced discriminatory treatment and restrictions on immigration.

  • London: Shyamji Krishna Varma established India House as a student residence and nationalist meeting place in 1905.
  • Paris and continental Europe: Madam Bhikaiji Cama appealed for India's freedom at international gatherings and distributed nationalist literature.
  • United States and Canada: Indian migrants and organisers built the Ghadar movement, while the Komagata Maru incident of 1914 exposed racial exclusion in Canada.

A person, a political association, a student hostel, a newspaper and a ship incident are different historical categories. India House, the Ghadar Party and Komagata Maru should not be treated as interchangeable organisations.

Prelims focus

  • India House was associated with Indian students and nationalism in London.
  • The Ghadar movement developed among overseas Indians in North America.
  • The Komagata Maru incident concerned immigration into Canada in 1914.
  • Trap: Revolutionaries abroad did not all belong to one organisation.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 112–115; IGNOU, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, The Revolutionaries, sections 9.1–9.3, printed pp. 116–120; consulted in the GPSC Books library and on IGNOU eGyanKosh, 21 November 2026.]

title: Why Indian revolutionaries organised abroad

body:
A revolutionary with a Gujarat connection

Shyamji Krishna Varma (also spelt Verma) was born in Mandvi, Kutch, in present-day Gujarat. A Sanskrit scholar, lawyer and Indian nationalist, he made London a centre of his campaign against British rule. His importance lies in building institutions through which Indians abroad could study, meet and argue for self-government and national freedom.

Three connected but distinct institutions in 1905

Varma's activities in London are best understood by distinguishing the purposes of three names commonly associated with him:

  • Indian Home Rule Society: a political association formed in London in 1905 to promote the cause of self-rule for India.
  • India House: a residence for Indian students opened in 1905 at Highgate, London. It became an important meeting centre for nationalist and revolutionary ideas.
  • The Indian Sociologist: a journal started by Varma in 1905 to circulate political criticism of British rule and arguments for Indian freedom.

These activities reinforced one another. A student residence brought people together; an association provided a political platform; and a journal carried arguments beyond those who could attend meetings in person. The house subsequently became associated with revolutionaries such as V. D. Savarkar. Varma relocated to Paris in 1907 as British pressure on his political work grew.

A name that must not be confused

The Indian Home Rule Society of 1905 was Varma's London-based association. It was not the same as the Home Rule Leagues associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant in India in 1916. The similarity of names does not make them one institution.

Prelims focus

  • Shyamji Krishna Varma came from Mandvi in Kutch, Gujarat.
  • He founded the Indian Home Rule Society in London in 1905.
  • India House opened at Highgate, London, in 1905 and served Indian students.
  • The Indian Sociologist was Varma's journal, not a student hostel.
  • Varma moved his base to Paris in 1907.
  • Trap: The Indian Home Rule Society (1905) and the Home Rule Leagues (1916) were different organisations.

[Sources: District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, Shyamji Krishna Verma Memorial, biographical section (consulted 21 November 2026); Krantiguru Shyamji Krishna Verma Kachchh University, About Krantiguru Shyamji Krishna Verma, sections on the Indian Home Rule Society and India House (consulted 21 November 2026); South Asian Britain: Connecting Histories, Shyamaji Krishnavarma and India House entries, sections on their founding (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Varma connected a political association, a student centre and a journal in London.

title: Shyamji Krishna Varma and India House in London

body:
Political work across European cities

Madam Bhikaiji Cama was an Indian nationalist born in Bombay in 1861. During her stay in London, she came into contact with Indian nationalists including Shyamji Krishna Varma and Dadabhai Naoroji. She supported the overseas campaign for self-rule and was involved with the Indian Home Rule Society in London in 1905. Her subsequent political work was closely associated with Paris, where she helped build the Paris Indian Society and circulated material supporting India's independence.

Cama's work shows that the overseas movement was not limited to secret meetings or student residences. It also involved presenting India's demand for freedom to international audiences.

The Stuttgart event of 1907

On 22 August 1907, at the International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany, Cama appealed for India's freedom and displayed an early Indian independence flag. The act gave the Indian nationalist cause visibility at a gathering outside the British Empire.

The flag associated with Cama in 1907 was an unofficial flag of the freedom struggle. It must not be identified as the national flag that India adopted on 22 July 1947. Stuttgart was the site of the international event; London and Paris were centres of Cama's political activity.

How Cama relates to India House

Cama belonged to overlapping circles of overseas nationalists, including people associated with Shyamji Krishna Varma. But Varma founded India House; Cama is especially remembered for spreading India's cause in Europe and for the Stuttgart flag event. The two contributions are connected but should not be exchanged in person–achievement questions.

Prelims focus

  • Madam Bhikaiji Cama was born in Bombay in 1861.
  • She worked with overseas Indian nationalists in London and Paris.
  • She displayed an early independence flag at Stuttgart, Germany, on 22 August 1907.
  • The event was the International Socialist Congress.
  • Trap: The 1907 flag was not the present national flag of India.

[Sources: New India Samachar, 16–31 August 2022, Bhikaiji Cama: She Unfurled the Indian Flag for the First Time on Foreign Soil, printed p. 49, Press Information Bureau publication (consulted 21 November 2026); IGNOU, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, section 9.2.2, printed p. 118 (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: A woman delegate presents a partly folded, unmarked freedom-struggle flag to seated delegates in a period congress hall in Stuttgart in 1907.
pictures.caption: A public appeal for Indian freedom at the Stuttgart congress in 1907.

title: Madam Bhikaiji Cama and the flag at Stuttgart

body:
Why the Ghadar movement developed

Ghadar means rebellion or revolt. In the years before the First World War, Indian migrants on the Pacific Coast of North America faced racial prejudice and restrictive immigration laws. Many were workers and former soldiers from Punjab. For some migrants, the denial of equal treatment abroad reinforced the belief that Indians would not be respected while India remained under British rule.

From this setting emerged the Ghadar Party in 1913, a revolutionary nationalist organisation whose central aim was to end British rule in India. Although a large number of its supporters were Punjabi Sikhs, its political appeal was to Indians across religious communities.

Organisation and leading figures

The organisation initially operated under the name Hindi Association of the Pacific Coast, also rendered in textbooks as Pacific Coast Hindustan Association. It is best known as the Ghadar Party. The important distinctions among its early leaders are:

PersonRole or association
Lala Har DayalLeading organiser and general secretary
Sohan Singh BhaknaFirst president
Pandit Kanshi RamEarly treasurer

San Francisco, United States, became the movement's principal headquarters. Its organisational and publishing centre was known as Yugantar Ashram. San Francisco was the headquarters; it should not be assumed that every early organisational meeting took place there.

The newspaper named Ghadar

The movement also issued a newspaper called Ghadar, first published from San Francisco on 1 November 1913. The first edition appeared in Urdu; a Punjabi edition in Gurmukhi script followed. The paper later circulated in other languages and among Indian communities beyond North America. It spread criticism of colonial rule and urged readers to work for India's freedom.

The Ghadar Party was the organisation; Ghadar was also its newspaper. Neither should be confused with The Indian Sociologist, the London-based journal associated with Shyamji Krishna Varma.

World War I and the attempt to revolt

When the First World War began in 1914, the Ghadar leaders saw Britain's wartime difficulties as a possible opportunity. They urged overseas Indians to return to India and encourage opposition, including among Indian soldiers. The attempts at an uprising were disrupted and suppressed by 1915. Thus, the party's founding in 1913 and the later wartime revolutionary attempt are related but different events.

Prelims focus

  • The Ghadar Party arose among Indian migrants on the Pacific Coast in 1913.
  • Lala Har Dayal was a leading organiser; Sohan Singh Bhakna was its first president.
  • Yugantar Ashram was its headquarters in San Francisco.
  • The Ghadar newspaper began on 1 November 1913, initially in Urdu.
  • World War I began in 1914 and encouraged the Ghadar call for revolt in India.
  • Trap: The Ghadar Party and the Ghadar newspaper shared a name but were not the same type of institution.

[Sources: Government of Tamil Nadu, State Council of Educational Research and Training, History, Class 12, Volume 1, first edition 2019, Unit 3, Impact of World War I on Indian Freedom Movement, printed p. 35; IGNOU, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, sections 9.3–9.4, printed pp. 119–123; New India Samachar, 16–31 March 2023, Pandit Kanshiram, printed p. 49; online sources consulted 21 November 2026.]
